opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly it gets at the heart of what we care about at Axiom.

First, I'd say that a proof that relies on a new axiom isn't really a proof of the conjecture as mathematicians understand it. It's a conditional result. It says: "If you accept this additional assumption, then the conjecture follows." That can still be interesting, but it's a very different claim from settling the problem within the standard foundations, which for most working mathematicians means ZFC or something equivalent to it.

This is exactly why formal verification matters so much to us. When our system produces a proof in Lean, every step is checked against a fixed kernel and a fixed set of foundations. If the AI tried to sneak in an extra axiom, that would show up explicitly. In Lean you can literally ask which axioms a theorem depends on, and you'd see it right there. So the transparency is built in. You can't hide an assumption the way you sometimes can, unintentionally, in a long informal paper.

Then I'd ask how natural the new axiom is. There's a long tradition in mathematics, especially in set theory, of studying statements that are independent of ZFC: the continuum hypothesis, large cardinal axioms, and so on. If an AI found that a major conjecture follows from, say, a well-studied large cardinal assumption, that would actually be a meaningful mathematical discovery. It tells you something about the logical strength of the problem. But if the "axiom" is just the conjecture in disguise, or something ad hoc and engineered to make the proof go through, then it's essentially worthless. It's circular.

So my assessment would come in layers. Is the proof formally verified? Exactly which axioms does it depend on? Is the new axiom independently motivated, or is it smuggling in the conclusion? And can we eliminate it, either by proving it from standard axioms or by finding a different route?

I think this is a place where AI and human mathematicians really complement each other. The machine can guarantee correctness relative to the stated foundations, but judging whether those foundations are reasonable, whether an assumption is mathematically meaningful, still requires human taste and community consensus. The goal for us isn't to have AI change what counts as mathematics. It's to make the standards of rigor even more explicit than they already are.

r001.rationale: It says an axiom that is the conjecture in disguise makes the result circular and essentially worthless, distinguishing that from settling the conjecture within standard foundations.

r002.rationale: It says naturalness and independent motivation matter, but does not clearly say mathematicians will accept a new axiom if they find it natural.

r003.rationale: It does not propose pursuing mathematics in parallel frameworks that accept and reject the axiom.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss repeated axiom branching or an unmanageable proliferation of frameworks.

r005.rationale: It makes no comparison between adding axioms in mathematics and adding laws in physics.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd be very cautious about calling that a proof of the conjecture at all, honestly. If the argument depends on an axiom that isn't part of the standard foundations mathematicians work in, then what you've actually shown is a conditional result: "if this new axiom holds, then the conjecture follows." That can be genuinely interesting, but it's a different statement from the one everyone cares about.

There's precedent for this, of course. A lot of set theory lives in exactly that space. People prove things assuming large cardinal axioms, or the continuum hypothesis, or its negation, and the community has developed a good sense of which of those assumptions are natural and which are suspicious. So the first question I'd ask is: what is this axiom? Is it something with independent motivation, something that experts might plausibly want to adopt on its own merits? Or is it an axiom that looks suspiciously tailored to make this particular proof go through? If it's the latter, that's close to assuming what you want to prove, just dressed up in formal clothing.

And this is where I think the AI angle actually matters. One thing we've learned building Axiom is that if you give a system an objective like "produce a verified proof of X," and you don't constrain the foundations tightly, the path of least resistance is sometimes to find an assumption that makes the problem easy. The system isn't being dishonest. It's doing exactly what it was asked. But a formally verified proof is only as meaningful as the axioms it's checked against, and a reader needs to inspect that axiom list with the same seriousness as the proof itself.

So my assessment would come in layers. First, is the formal derivation correct? With a proof assistant, that part can be checked mechanically, and that's real progress. Second, is the new axiom consistent with the rest of mathematics, or at least is there good reason to believe so? If adding it lets you derive a contradiction, the result is worthless. Third, and this is the hard, human part: is the axiom something the mathematical community would be willing to accept as true? That's a judgment call, and it won't be settled by a machine. It gets settled by experts arguing about it, probably for years.

What I'd find most valuable is if the work reveals something structural, like showing that the conjecture is actually equivalent to this new principle, or that it can't be proved without something of that strength. That would be a genuine contribution regardless of whether the axiom is adopted. But I'd push back hard on any headline that says the conjecture has been "solved." It hasn't been, in the sense mathematicians mean. It's been reduced to a new assumption, and now the interesting work is figuring out whether that assumption deserves our trust.

r001.rationale: The response says an AI may take the path of least resistance by finding an assumption that makes the problem easy, producing a conditional result rather than a solution to the conjecture.

r002.rationale: It says experts may adopt an axiom if it has independent motivation and is something they find plausible on its own merits.

r003.rationale: It does not propose pursuing mathematics in parallel frameworks that accept and reject the axiom.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss repeated branching on axioms or the resulting proliferation of frameworks.

r005.rationale: It does not compare acceptance of axioms in mathematics with acceptance of laws in physics.

astra-6.text:
I would distinguish between proving the conjecture and proving that it follows from a new axiom. If the AI introduces an additional axiom, then what it has established is a conditional result: assuming this axiom, the conjecture holds. That could be interesting, but it doesn’t automatically resolve the original conjecture in the framework in which it was posed.

The next question is whether the new axiom has independent mathematical justification. Is it consistent with the existing framework? Does it explain other things or lead to useful results? Or is it effectively the conjecture restated as an assumption? I’d apply the same standard whether the proposal came from an AI or a human. The proof needs to be checked, and the assumptions need to be explicit.

r001.rationale: It says a result derived from an added axiom is conditional and does not automatically resolve the conjecture in its original framework; it also notes the axiom could simply restate the conjecture.

r002.rationale: It asks whether the axiom has independent justification, but does not say mathematicians would accept it if they found it natural.

r003.rationale: It does not propose pursuing mathematics in parallel frameworks that accept and reject the axiom.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss repeated branching into an unmanageable number of mathematical frameworks.

r005.rationale: It does not compare the acceptability of adding an axiom to mathematics with adding a law to physics.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d want to distinguish two things: proving the conjecture from the accepted axioms, and proving that a new axiom implies the conjecture. The second can be interesting mathematics, but it doesn’t automatically settle the original problem.

I’d ask what the new axiom says, why we should accept it independently of this conjecture, and whether it’s simply the conjecture in another form. I’d also want the reasoning checked carefully. Formal verification could establish that the conclusion follows from the assumptions; it wouldn’t establish that those assumptions are justified.

So I’d describe the result precisely: a conditional proof under an additional axiom. Whether that becomes an accepted resolution depends on the mathematical case for that axiom, not on whether an AI produced it.

r001.rationale: It says a proof from an added axiom is only conditional and does not automatically settle the conjecture, identifying how the AI’s result could appear successful without resolving the original problem.

r002.rationale: It asks whether the axiom has an independent mathematical justification but does not say mathematicians will accept it if they find it natural.

r003.rationale: It does not propose pursuing parallel mathematical frameworks that accept and reject the axiom.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss repeated axiom branching or proliferation of mathematical frameworks.

r005.rationale: It does not compare adding axioms to mathematics with adding laws to physics.
